edits.old: To ask which of these haplotypes are present in cultivated barley, we compared five European spring malting cultivars released between 2012 and 2018 with the wild haplotype groups at the same three genes (Fig. 3d–f; Online Resource 10). At *GPAT6*, the five cultivars matched the two low-fiber haplotype groups at 95–98% and 88–91% of called sites but the high-fiber group at only 39–45%, so the high-fiber wild haplotype is essentially absent from these lines. The cultivars, like the two low-fiber groups, carried the reference (Morex) allele at only 12–14% of these sites, against 65% in the high-fiber group. At *GH17* and *PHT4;3*, by contrast, all five cultivars carried the reference allele at every called site. <!-- R3 (Results voice review, 2026-10-01): same numbers; method and figure-drawing clauses removed ('genotyped … from an independent MorexV3 call set', 'drawn beneath'; the M&M describes both); gene names instead of 'the acyltransferase / glucanase / phosphate transporter' (the short names are introduced in the three paragraphs above). --> <!-- src: 07_USED_elite_lines_compariosn_to_wild_lines/results/tables/results_chapter_numbers.txt (5 lines, released 2012-2018, IPK DivBrowse barley pangenome v2 called against MorexV3; crosshap not re-run and never saw the elite lines) + Table_site_overlap.tsv (shared 43/33/12 of wild 54/41/16; monomorphic among the 5 lines at 42 of 43, 33 of 33 and 12 of 12 kept sites - the basis of "near-identical to one another") + README.md "What the figures show" (agreements recomputed 2026-09-23 from Table_elite_genotypes_wide__*.tsv: GPAT6 group A 95-98%, group B 88-91%, group C 39-45%; elite %REF 12-13% vs group A 14%, B 12%, C 65%; GH17 and PHT4;3 100% REF at every called site) -->

edits.old: In the haplotype analysis, the gene resolved into two haplotype groups over 246 of the 290 accessions, with the same grouping for both traits (Fig. 4; Online Resource 9). The haplotypes were defined by a single marker group of four SNPs: the three significant SNPs and a fourth in linkage disequilibrium with them (7H:573,606,282; r² = 0.44–0.54). The minority haplotype B comprised exactly the 34 accessions carrying the minor allele at both lead SNPs. It had higher fiber (*P* = 2.1 × 10⁻³, η² = 0.035, 0.54 SD; Fig. 4a) and lower starch (*P* = 1.1 × 10⁻³, η² = 0.040, 0.56 SD; Fig. 4b) than the major haplotype A (*n* = 212). Thus, a single haplotype at this gene was associated with both traits in opposite directions, matching the negative phenotypic correlation between fiber and starch (Fig. 1c). At the four SNPs that defined the haplotypes, the five elite malting cultivars carried the alleles of the low-fiber, high-starch haplotype A at every called site, and none carried those of the high-fiber, low-starch haplotype B (Fig. 4c).
